opus-5.5.text:
For me, the dream is having AI take on the parts of mathematics that are hugely time-consuming but not where the real insight lives. When you're working on a research problem, so much of the effort goes into checking cases, verifying lemmas, chasing down whether some estimate actually holds, or digging through the literature to find out whether someone already proved a version of what you need thirty years ago in a paper nobody reads anymore. Those things can eat weeks or months.

So the first thing I'd love is a really reliable collaborator for verification. That's why I'm so excited about formal proof systems like Lean. If an AI could take a sketch of an argument, the way mathematicians actually write on a whiteboard, and turn it into a fully verified formal proof, that changes the trust model of mathematics. You wouldn't need a handful of experts spending a year refereeing a two-hundred-page paper. You'd know it's correct.

The second thing, and this is more ambitious, is exploration. In number theory and combinatorics, a lot of progress comes from staring at examples and noticing patterns. An AI that can generate conjectures, test them at scale, and say "this looks true, and here's a structural reason it might be" would be an incredible partner. It's not about replacing the mathematician's taste. It's about widening the space you can explore before you decide what's worth your attention.

Ultimately I'd like AI to be something like a tireless, very knowledgeable graduate student who never gets bored and never makes arithmetic mistakes, so the human can spend more time on the questions of which problems matter and why.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing I'd most want help with isn't the glamorous part. It's the grind.

When you're working on a hard problem, maybe eighty percent of the time goes to things that aren't the key idea. You have a conjecture, and you need to check it against twenty examples before you trust it enough to try proving it. You need to verify that a lemma you half-remember from a paper actually says what you think it says, with the exact hypotheses. You need to carry a long computation through without dropping a sign. None of that is where the insight lives, but if you get it wrong, you waste a week.

So the first thing I'd want is a collaborator that's tireless at verification. Something that can take a sketch of an argument and tell me, rigorously, where the gaps are. Not "this looks plausible," but "step four assumes compactness and you never established it." That's what formal systems like Lean are starting to make possible, and I think it changes the social contract of mathematics. Right now, trust in a proof depends on a handful of experts reading it carefully. If a machine can check it, you can be far more ambitious about what you attempt, because the cost of being wrong goes down.

The second thing is search. The literature is enormous and fragmented. There are results sitting in a 1970s paper in a different subfield that would solve someone's problem today, and nobody knows because the vocabulary is different. An AI that genuinely understands the mathematics, not just the keywords, could connect those. I think a lot of "new" theorems are going to turn out to be rediscoveries once that kind of search works well.

And then the third thing, the one I'm most curious about, is whether it can propose. Not prove the Riemann hypothesis. Just say, "here's a definition that would make these three messy results look like one clean statement." Good definitions are the rarest thing in math. If a system could even occasionally offer a useful one, that would be a real partner rather than a tool.

What I don't want is something that hands me a finished proof I can't understand. The point isn't just to know a theorem is true. The point is to understand why. If AI gets us the truth without the understanding, I'd consider that a partial failure, even if the theorem count goes up.

Even a failed approach can be useful if it reveals something about the problem. I’d love a collaborator that helps me build intuition, alongside checking the details of an argument.
